analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set enforceable national limits on PFAS 'forever chemicals' in drinking water.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship, the bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without ever getting a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Environmental Protection Agency, within two years, to set a maximum contaminant level for PFAS — man-made 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick cookware, weatherproof clothing, and firefighting foam that may harm human health [S2]. Communities across the country, including areas near military bases and chemical plants, have found these chemicals in their drinking water. It also directed the EPA to ease monitoring burdens for clean water systems and to prioritize federal technical help and funding for small, rural, and disadvantaged water systems trying to comply [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households that drink public water. An enforceable national limit would mean every water system must test for PFAS and treat water that exceeds the standard, protecting residents — especially those near industrial sites and military installations — from exposure linked to health risks [S2]. Small, rural, and disadvantaged systems would get priority federal help to comply rather than bearing the cost alone [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA to set a maximum contaminant level and a national drinking water regulation for PFAS within two years of enactment, replacing the absence of an enforceable standard.
Prioritizes existing federal technical assistance and funding for small, rural, or disadvantaged public water systems so the compliance burden does not fall entirely on their ratepayers.
Lets the EPA tailor monitoring rules for water systems that consistently test below the limit, sparing clean systems unnecessary testing costs.

analysis.who_pays: PFAS chemical manufacturers, whose products are the source of drinking water contamination and who would face stronger cleanup and liability pressure once an enforceable national limit exists, and water utilities and their ratepayers, who would bear testing and treatment costs — though the bill directs federal assistance to small and disadvantaged systems.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS chemical makers and water utilities

drawbacks.text: A national PFAS limit would impose real monitoring and treatment costs on public water systems, which would fall partly on ratepayers through water bills; the bill directs funding toward small and disadvantaged systems but does not itself appropriate money to cover the mandate.

The bill sets drinking water standards only; it does not ban PFAS in consumer products such as nonstick cookware and weatherproof clothing, so the chemicals would continue entering the environment at the source.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a binding national ceiling on toxic chemicals in the water people drink — is substantial and addresses contamination that communities currently have no federal standard to force action on. The main cost is compliance spending by water utilities, which the bill partially offsets by prioritizing help for small and disadvantaged systems and by easing monitoring for already-clean systems. A fair-minded criticism is that the bill regulates at the tap rather than at the source, leaving PFAS makers free to keep putting the chemicals into products and the environment.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2019 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, the bill sat there; the committee never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill on May 15, 2019, co-introduced with Senator Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, a state whose residents were at the center of the PFAS water contamination crisis.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day it was introduced.
Five senators cosponsored it — four Democrats and one Republican — but no further action was ever recorded on the bill in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and heavy users of the chemicals came out ahead: with the bill dead, no enforceable national drinking water limit was put in place during the 116th Congress, and water systems avoided new compliance costs for the time being. Residents of communities with PFAS-contaminated water gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS chemical makers; contaminated communities gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, requiring the EPA to set a national PFAS drinking water limit within two years.

for.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Gillibrand, giving it bipartisan sponsorship at introduction.

for.name: 5 Senate cosponsors (4 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Added their names to the bill; no cosponsor acted further to move it.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2019 and never reported it out, held no vote on it, and let it die when the 116th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so opposition was never recorded; the bill began with bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic lead sponsor, a Republican co-introducer from a heavily affected state, and five cosponsors split 4 Democrats to 1 Republican.

industries.note: A national drinking water limit does not directly regulate these manufacturers, but it creates the enforceable standard that underpins cleanup requirements and liability for PFAS they put into the environment. With the bill dead, they faced no new federal limit during the 116th Congress.

The bill would have required utilities to monitor for and treat PFAS to meet the new limit, a real cost passed partly to ratepayers — but it also prioritized federal technical assistance and funding for small, rural, and disadvantaged systems and eased monitoring for already-clean systems.

industries.industry: Makers of PFAS-containing consumer products (nonstick cookware, weatherproof clothing)
industries.note: The bill does not ban these products, but an official finding behind a national water limit would increase scrutiny of the chemicals in them. The products would have remained on the market regardless.
